old.name: Le Marais
old.hook: A dense weave of medieval lanes and Renaissance mansions (hôtels particuliers), the Jewish Pletzl around Rue des Rosiers, the Carnavalet and Picasso museums, and the city's oldest cafe-lined stone.
old.text: A dense weave of medieval lanes and Renaissance mansions (hôtels particuliers), the Jewish Pletzl around Rue des Rosiers, the Carnavalet and Picasso museums, and the city's oldest cafe-lined stone. The name means marsh, and that is literal: low, wet ground drained from the 12th century onward by the Knights Templar (Louis VII granted them the land in 1139) and religious orders. It turned aristocratic the moment Place des Vosges opened in 1612, then emptied when the court decamped to Versailles, and decayed for two centuries. The paradox that saved it: too poor to be worth demolishing, its 17th-century mansions were still standing when André Malraux made the Marais France's first protected 'secteur sauvegardé' in 1964. Signal marsh drained from 1139, France's first protected heritage sector 1964

old.name: Canal Saint-Martin
old.hook: A 4.5km canal of nine locks, arched iron footbridges and plane trees, its quays now lined with bistros and booksellers.
old.text: A 4.5km canal of nine locks, arched iron footbridges and plane trees, its quays now lined with bistros and booksellers. Napoleon ordered it dug in 1802 and paid for it with a tax on wine, for a blunt reason: to pipe clean water into a city dying of cholera and dysentery, and to float in grain and stone. It was finished in 1825; Napoleon III later roofed over nearly half of it to lay boulevards on top. The still green water and the swing-bridges are the ones Amelie skips stones across in the 2001 film, and the Hotel du Nord still standing on the quay gave French cinema its immortal cry of 'Atmosphere!' in 1938. Signal ordered by Napoleon 1802, completed 1825

old_also.name: Canal Saint-Martin
old_also.hook: A 4.5 km canal of iron footbridges and stepped double locks, its plane-tree quais the Sunday-evening living room of the 10th — Parisians sit on the stone edge with cheese, a baguette and a bottle while boats grind up through the locks.
old_also.text: A 4.5 km canal of iron footbridges and stepped double locks, its plane-tree quais the Sunday-evening living room of the 10th — Parisians sit on the stone edge with cheese, a baguette and a bottle while boats grind up through the locks. The terroir is the water that stopped killing Parisians. By 1802 the city drank from the same Seine it dumped its sewage into, and cholera and dysentery did the rest. Napoleon ordered a canal to pipe clean water in from the river Ourcq — and to pay for it the state taxed wine, so Parisians quite literally drank their way to clean water. It opened in 1825, four years after Napoleon died in exile. About half its length was later roofed over under Napoleon III (the tree-lined Boulevard Richard-Lenoir runs above the covered stretch). The one real thing: this is the anti-Seine — no monuments, barely a tour boat, just the neighbourhood at its own aperitif rituals. Signal Ordered by Napoleon in 1802, opened 1825, funded by a wine tax (verified: Wikipedia, Life in Rural France)

old.name: Belleville
old.hook: A steep, gloriously multi-ethnic working-class quarter climbing above the city, with a Chinatown, North African and Jewish shops, dense street art, and the terraced Parc de Belleville.
old.text: A steep, gloriously multi-ethnic working-class quarter climbing above the city, with a Chinatown, North African and Jewish shops, dense street art, and the terraced Parc de Belleville. Once a village of vineyards and open-air guinguettes, it was annexed in 1860 and promptly filled with the workers Haussmann's demolitions had pushed out of central Paris, then wave after wave of immigrants. Edith Piaf grew up singing in these streets; legend has her born under a lamppost on Rue de Belleville in 1915, though the honest record puts her birth at the Hôpital Tenon nearby. The reward for the climb: the terrace of Parc de Belleville, opened 1988 on the neighbourhood's 108m hill, is one of the highest free viewpoints in Paris. Signal annexed 1860, Piaf born in the quarter 1915, park terrace opened 1988

quartiers:Montmartre & the Butte.group: The hill and the Left Bank

old.name: Montmartre & the Butte
old.hook: Paris's high point at 130m, crowned by the white domes of Sacre-Coeur, laced with stairs and the Clos Montmartre — the city's most famous surviving vineyard, replanted by the City of Paris in 1933 — above the tourist easels of Place du Tertre.
old.text: Paris's high point at 130m, crowned by the white domes of Sacre-Coeur, laced with stairs and the Clos Montmartre — the city's most famous surviving vineyard, replanted by the City of Paris in 1933 — above the tourist easels of Place du Tertre. A martyr's hill: Saint Denis, first bishop of Paris, was said to be beheaded here around 250 AD, giving Mont des Martyrs its name. It stayed a village of gypsum quarries and vineyards until Paris annexed it in 1860, and its cheap rents then drew Renoir, Toulouse-Lautrec, Picasso and Van Gogh. Sacre-Coeur was begun in 1875 as national penance for the defeat by Prussia and the bloodshed of the Commune. One real thing to know: 'plaster of Paris' is Montmartre gypsum, quarried out of this very hill until the mines wound down around annexation. Signal annexed to Paris 1860, Sacre-Coeur begun 1875

quartiers:Saint-Germain-des-Prés.group: The hill and the Left Bank

old.name: Saint-Germain-des-Prés
old.hook: The Left Bank's literary heart: the oldest church in Paris, the terraces of Cafe de Flore and Les Deux Magots, and the publishing houses that still cluster the surrounding streets.
old.text: The Left Bank's literary heart: the oldest church in Paris, the terraces of Cafe de Flore and Les Deux Magots, and the publishing houses that still cluster the surrounding streets. It grew around an abbey founded in the 6th century by Childebert I, son of Clovis, to shelter relics he brought back from the siege of Zaragoza — a fragment of the True Cross and Saint Vincent's tunic; the church was dedicated in 558, the very year the king died (23 December), and it became the burial place of the Merovingian dynasty. Fourteen centuries later its cafes became the headquarters of Sartre, de Beauvoir and post-war existentialism. What visitors miss: long before it was a philosophers' salon, the abbey's annual fair made this one of the great marketplaces of medieval Europe. Signal abbey founded c.543-558 (church dedicated 558), existentialist heyday 1940s-50s

old.name: Place des Vosges
old.hook: Paris's oldest planned square: a perfect 140m x 140m of matching red-brick-and-stone pavilions raised over vaulted arcades, wrapped around a garden of clipped limes and four fountains. Victor Hugo's apartment at No. 6 is now a museum whose permanent collection is free to visit.
old.text: Paris's oldest planned square: a perfect 140m x 140m of matching red-brick-and-stone pavilions raised over vaulted arcades, wrapped around a garden of clipped limes and four fountains. Victor Hugo's apartment at No. 6 is now a museum whose permanent collection is free to visit. Born in Paris · Sauce Sauce Bearnaise Credited to chef Jean-Louis-Francois Collinet, who is said to have served it at the 1836 opening of Le Pavillon Henri IV, a restaurant in Saint-Germain-en-Laye just west of Paris - reportedly a happy accident while working a shallot-and-butter emulsion off a broken hollandaise. He named it for Bearn, birthplace of Henri IV, whose former residence housed the restaurant. The accident tale is the traditional account rather than documented fact, and a similar recipe is said to predate 1836. Try it — Le Pavillon Henri IV in Saint-Germain-en-Laye (the origin site, still a hotel-restaurant); in Paris, order it alongside an entrecote at any classic bistro. A little Paris beauty · Cafe Le Procope Opened in 1686 by the Sicilian Procopio Cutò, who fitted his rooms with crystal chandeliers, wall mirrors and marble-topped tables — the template every European café would copy — Le Procope claims to be the oldest café in Paris. La Fontaine, Voltaire, Diderot's Encyclopédistes and later Danton and Franklin argued over coffee and ice cream here. Honest footnote: the original café shut in 1872 and the space reopened as a restaurant in 1957, so it is a restored shrine to the ritual rather than an unbroken 340-year pour. Where — 13 rue de l'Ancienne-Comédie, 6th arrondissement (also reachable through the Cour du Commerce Saint-André) It stands on grief. Here rose the Hôtel des Tournelles, the royal palace where Henri II died in 1559 after a lance splinter drove through his visor at a tournament; his widow Catherine de' Medici had the whole thing torn down. Henri IV built the square on the cleared ground from 1605 to 1612 and did something no French king had done before: he dictated that every house-front obey a single design, inventing the 'place royale'. It was inaugurated in 1612 with a carrousel for the boy Louis XIII's betrothal to Anne of Austria, and kept the name Place Royale until 1800, when it was renamed for the Vosges department, the first to remit its taxes to the young Republic. Signal built 1605-1612 by Henri IV, renamed Place des Vosges in 1800

old_also.name: Place des Vosges
old_also.hook: Paris's oldest planned square, completed 1612 under Henri IV (who commissioned it in 1605) — 36 matching pavilions of red brick and pale stone over vaulted arcades, laid out as one of Europe's first pieces of royal town planning. Victor Hugo lived at no. 6 from 1832 to 1848.
old_also.text: Paris's oldest planned square, completed 1612 under Henri IV (who commissioned it in 1605) — 36 matching pavilions of red brick and pale stone over vaulted arcades, laid out as one of Europe's first pieces of royal town planning. Victor Hugo lived at no. 6 from 1832 to 1848. Signal Straddling the 3e/4e in the Marais. The square and its arcades are free and always open; the Maison de Victor Hugo at no. 6 has a free permanent collection, closed Mondays. Bring a picnic from the nearby Marché des Enfants Rouges.

old.name: Place Dauphine
old.hook: A hushed, leaf-shaded triangle of brick-and-stone houses hidden at the western prow of the island, one of the quietest addresses in the middle of Paris.
old.text: A hushed, leaf-shaded triangle of brick-and-stone houses hidden at the western prow of the island, one of the quietest addresses in the middle of Paris. Henri IV's second royal square, and the reason it is a triangle and not a rectangle is honest geography: it fills the raw silt-spit at the tip of the Île de la Cité, just off his new Pont Neuf. On 10 March 1607 he handed roughly three acres to Achille de Harlay with a single condition, that every facade repeat the same model, and named the ensemble for the Dauphin, his six-year-old son and future Louis XIII. The last house was finished in 1616. Much altered since, but the triangle and its calm survive. Signal begun 1607 by Henri IV, houses completed by 1616

old.name: Place des Victoires
old.hook: A circular royal square, now ringed by fashion houses, with an equestrian Louis XIV rearing at its centre.
old.text: A circular royal square, now ringed by fashion houses, with an equestrian Louis XIV rearing at its centre. The only one of the great royal squares built not by a king but by a courtier's flattery. Maréchal de la Feuillade commissioned a gilded statue of Louis XIV after the Treaty of Nijmegen, then hired Jules Hardouin-Mansart to raise an entire round square around it (1685-86). The radius was set by the statue's own proportions, and the approaching streets were deliberately kept out of alignment so the king's effigy would always stand clear against the facades. What you teach a visitor here: the original — a standing figure of the king crowned by Victory, not a horseman — was melted down in the Revolution; the equestrian statue there today is Bosio's replacement of 1822. Signal designed 1685-1686 by Hardouin-Mansart, inaugurated by the Dauphin (standing in for the absent king) March 1686

old.name: Parc Rives de Seine (the car-free quais)
old.hook: The riverside expressway is gone. Both banks between the Musée d'Orsay and the Arsenal marina are now a car-free promenade — floating gardens planted on barges, café terraces, and stone steps down to the water where Parisians sit at dusk with a bottle.
old.text: The riverside expressway is gone. Both banks between the Musée d'Orsay and the Arsenal marina are now a car-free promenade — floating gardens planted on barges, café terraces, and stone steps down to the water where Parisians sit at dusk with a bottle. The terroir is the Seine taken back from cars. For decades the Voie Georges-Pompidou was a motorway welded to the river; you physically could not reach the water. Mayor Delanoë pedestrianised the left bank in 2013 — with five gardens floated on barges, moored near the Pont de l'Alma — and Hidalgo seized the right bank in 2017, against furious driver opposition that went all the way to the courts. The one real thing: this is the newest great walk in Paris and the most contested one, a live argument about who the river belongs to. Signal Left bank pedestrianised 2013 (Delanoë), right bank 2017 (Hidalgo) (verified: Wikipedia, Paris je t'aime)

old.name: Square du Vert-Galant
old.hook: A small triangular garden at the very prow of the Île de la Cité, reached by stairs down from the Pont Neuf, sitting at the river's natural level — a weeping willow at the point, a few benches, and the Seine forking around you on three sides. Arguably the single best place in Paris to sit.
old.text: A small triangular garden at the very prow of the Île de la Cité, reached by stairs down from the Pont Neuf, sitting at the river's natural level — a weeping willow at the point, a few benches, and the Seine forking around you on three sides. Arguably the single best place in Paris to sit. The terroir is medieval Paris, seven metres down. Most people cross the Pont Neuf above and never notice the stairs exist. The name honours Henri IV, the 'Vert-Galant' (green gallant — a wink at the ageing king's tireless string of mistresses), whose green-oxidised bronze statue rides on the bridge overhead. The one real thing to know: you're sitting at the original ground level of the old city, some seven metres below today's streets — the island was built up over the centuries. The square itself was made in 1884 by joining two silty islets to the Cité. Come at sunset; the willow and the splitting river are the whole point. Signal Created 1884; named for Henri IV, whose Pont Neuf was finished 1606 (inaugurated 1607) (verified: Wikipedia, Ville de Paris)

old.name: Coulée verte René-Dumont (Promenade Plantée)
old.hook: A 4.7 km green ribbon that runs from behind the Opéra Bastille to the edge of the Bois de Vincennes, the first stretch riding ten metres up on the brick arches of a dead railway viaduct (the vaults below are the Viaduc des Arts craft workshops). Rose arbours, bamboo, lavender, pergolas — and near silence above the traffic.
old.text: A 4.7 km green ribbon that runs from behind the Opéra Bastille to the edge of the Bois de Vincennes, the first stretch riding ten metres up on the brick arches of a dead railway viaduct (the vaults below are the Viaduc des Arts craft workshops). Rose arbours, bamboo, lavender, pergolas — and near silence above the traffic. The terroir here is a resurrected railway. Trains ran Bastille-to-Vincennes on this viaduct until 1969; when the line died, most cities would have demolished it. Instead landscape architect Jacques Vergely and architect Philippe Mathieux planted a garden along the top — the first project in the world to turn an elevated railway into an urban garden — and it opened in 1993. The one real thing to know, because everyone gets it backwards: this predates New York's High Line, which only opened in 2009, and its creators cite the Paris promenade as a precedent. Paris did it first. Signal Inaugurated 1993 — the first elevated railway turned into a park walkway (verified: Wikipedia, Secrets of Paris)

old.name: La Petite Ceinture
old.hook: The abandoned railway that once ringed all of Paris, now a chain of wild, sunken green corridors — rails still in the ballast, buddleia, brambles, even foxes — reopened in pieces. This is a rare central-Paris place that feels genuinely unmanicured: a ruin, not a garden.
old.text: The abandoned railway that once ringed all of Paris, now a chain of wild, sunken green corridors — rails still in the ballast, buddleia, brambles, even foxes — reopened in pieces. This is a rare central-Paris place that feels genuinely unmanicured: a ruin, not a garden. The terroir is the city's forgotten ring handed back to nature. Built from 1852 under the Second Empire to run freight and then passengers around the old walls, the Petite Ceinture was strangled by the new Métro after 1900 and closed to passengers in 1934 — then simply left. For decades nobody knew what to do with it, and the trench went feral: the 15th-arrondissement stretch alone now counts 200-plus wild plant species and 70 animal species over 1.5 km of old track. The one real thing to know: the longest continuous walk is in the 12th — about 1.6 km from rue de Charenton to avenue de Saint-Mandé, with a 200 m nature trail and a community garden. Go for the strangeness, not the polish. Signal Rail line closed to passengers 1934; nine sections walkable across nine arrondissements today (verified: Wikipedia, Ville de Paris, ASPCRF)

walks:Parc des Buttes-Chaumont.group: Parks, a garden and the dead

old.name: Parc des Buttes-Chaumont
old.hook: A dramatic, hilly park with a cliff-ringed lake, a suspension footbridge, and a miniature Roman temple perched on a crag — the Temple de la Sibylle — that gives the best free view over the east of Paris. Locals sprawl on the steep lawns; this is where the 19th actually suns itself.
old.text: A dramatic, hilly park with a cliff-ringed lake, a suspension footbridge, and a miniature Roman temple perched on a crag — the Temple de la Sibylle — that gives the best free view over the east of Paris. Locals sprawl on the steep lawns; this is where the 19th actually suns itself. The terroir is faked geology built on a cursed hill. This was the Gibbet of Montfaucon, where from the 13th century to 1760 the bodies of the hanged were displayed to rot; afterwards a refuse dump and a yard for cutting up horse carcasses. Napoleon III and engineer Adolphe Alphand turned the most reviled ground in Paris into a park for the new working-class districts — blasting the exhausted gypsum quarry into cliffs, trucking in topsoil, and topping the 50-metre crag with Gabriel Davioud's temple copied from the one at Tivoli. It opened for the 1867 Exposition Universelle. Signal Opened 1 April 1867; built on the medieval gibbet of Montfaucon and a spent gypsum quarry (verified: Wikipedia, napoleon.org)

walks:Cimetière du Père-Lachaise.group: Parks, a garden and the dead

old.name: Cimetière du Père-Lachaise
old.hook: The largest cemetery in Paris is also one of its great walks: 44 cobbled, chestnut-shaded hectares climbing a hillside, where you pass between cats, moss and the tombs of Chopin, Wilde, Piaf and Proust. Go for the upper avenues, not the celebrity graves — that's where Parisians actually stroll on a Sunday.
old.text: The largest cemetery in Paris is also one of its great walks: 44 cobbled, chestnut-shaded hectares climbing a hillside, where you pass between cats, moss and the tombs of Chopin, Wilde, Piaf and Proust. Go for the upper avenues, not the celebrity graves — that's where Parisians actually stroll on a Sunday. The terroir is a marketing trick that worked. When Napoleon opened it in 1804 on the old estate of Louis XIV's confessor (Père La Chaise — hence the name), Parisians refused to be buried so far from the city, and it drew barely any funerals. So in 1817 the administrators staged a stunt — they paraded in the supposed bones of Molière and La Fontaine, and the purported remains of the medieval lovers Héloïse and Abélard under a canopy of salvaged abbey stone. It worked cynically well: over 33,000 graves by 1830. The honest caveat the guides skip: none of those relics are secure — historians doubt La Fontaine's body ever left its first cemetery, and 'Héloïse & Abélard' are recorded only as 'purported' remains. Signal Opened 1804; jumpstarted in 1817 by relocating 'Molière, La Fontaine' and 'Héloïse & Abélard' (verified: Wikipedia, napoleon.org, Mental Floss)

walks:Jardin du Palais-Royal.group: Parks, a garden and the dead

old.name: Jardin du Palais-Royal
old.hook: A perfect rectangle of clipped limes and rose beds enclosed by silent 18th-century arcades, hidden a block from the Louvre — with Daniel Buren's field of black-and-white striped columns in the forecourt. Office workers eat lunch on the fountain rim in near quiet.
old.text: A perfect rectangle of clipped limes and rose beds enclosed by silent 18th-century arcades, hidden a block from the Louvre — with Daniel Buren's field of black-and-white striped columns in the forecourt. Office workers eat lunch on the fountain rim in near quiet. The terroir is stillness on top of gunpowder. Cardinal Richelieu built the palace in the 1630s; a later Duc d'Orléans lined the garden with arcades of shops to clear his debts, and it became the pre-Revolutionary heart of Paris — cafés, gambling, radical pamphlets. It was here, at the Café de Foy, that Camille Desmoulins leapt onto a table on 12 July 1789 and called Paris to arms, two days before the Bastille fell. Colette wrote in an apartment above the garden until her death (the Allée Colette carries her name). In 1985–86, under Culture Minister Jack Lang, Daniel Buren filled the honour court with 260 candy-striped columns over the ventilation shafts — a national scandal then, a selfie shrine now. Signal Garden of Richelieu's 1630s palace; Buren's 'Les Deux Plateaux' (260 columns) installed 1985–86 under Jack Lang (verified: Secrets of Paris, fr.wikipedia)
